notes:
Here are my notes on Jeremiah 25. I couldn't cover everything you asked for. My searches ran out early, and the Matthew Henry page came back without its text, so for him I only have the search preview. The main sources are David Guzik (Enduring Word), Thomas Constable (dispensational), the StudyLight and BibleHub verse pages (Calvin, Gill, Keil & Delitzsch, Benson, Poole, Barnes, Pulpit and others), Coffman and Kingcomments. **I found nothing from Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace sources, so those sections are left out.** Where I quote Guzik or Constable directly from their pages, the URL is given in brackets.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** The fourth year of Jehoiakim was 605 BC. That year the Egyptians were defeated at Carchemish, and Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem but had to go home quickly when his father died. G. Campbell Morgan thought Jeremiah repeated this earlier prophecy as part of his message to Zedekiah. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/] Constable says the timing mattered: power had just shifted from Assyria to Babylon, and the people would have wondered what that meant for them. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-25.html] Benson points out that this prophecy came at least six or seven years before that in the preceding chapter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-25.html

**v. 2:** Guzik notes that the message was for all the people, even though few accepted it. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/]

**v. 3:** The 23 years were nineteen years under Josiah and four years under Jehoiakim (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html). Guzik notes Jeremiah was only a little past the halfway point of his ministry.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/ Matthew Henry says Jeremiah was a faithful, hard-working preacher who could appeal to the people's own memory of that.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_025.cfm Calvin works out that Jeremiah spoke these words 17 years before the city fell, and that he laboured for about forty years in all.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-25.html

**v. 4:** Constable names some of the other true prophets of the time: Uriah, Zephaniah and Habakkuk. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-25.html] The phrase "rising early" (KJV) stresses how urgent and dedicated the prophets were.  https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/25.htm

**vv. 5–6:** Two readings of "the works of your hands": Thompson (quoted by Guzik) says it may mean idols, or simply what the people do. Constable also calls the phrase ambiguous. [enduringword; studylight dcc, URLs above] Kingcomments says God promised not to harm them if they stopped.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

**v. 7:** Guzik says that by ignoring the prophets the people were rejecting God himself, and that this stubbornness provoked his anger. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/]

**vv. 8–9:**
- "Families of the north": Feinberg (quoted by Guzik) lists several possible meanings and prefers "the Babylonians in general".
- "My servant": Nebuchadnezzar was the instrument of judgment, not someone God approved of. Trapp calls him God's executioner. Guzik also notes that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) leaves out "My servant". [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/]
- Constable compares Nebuchadnezzar with Cyrus: a servant who did God's will mostly without knowing it. Because the people ignored God's servants the prophets, God sent a different kind of servant. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-25.html]
- "Perpetual" (everlasting) desolation: Calvin says the word in this context means the opposite of a short time, and is limited here by the seventy years.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-25.html Benson agrees, comparing a servant who serves "for ever", which the Jews took to mean "till the next jubilee." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-25.html

**v. 10:** Clarke (quoted by Guzik) says a land without the sound of millstones or the light of a lamp must be empty. Cundall describes it as an eerie silence and darkness. [enduringword] Constable says these images all mean the end of ordinary life. He also quotes Francis Schaeffer: when praying for his own culture, Schaeffer asked for mercy, not justice. [studylight dcc]

**v. 11:** The seventy years.
- Some see it as a round number: Harrison reckons it roughly from 605 to 536 BC. 
- Others, such as Feinberg, take it as exact, partly because Daniel knew he had been in Babylon for seventy years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/
- Link to the Sabbath years: The number matches the land-rest Sabbath cycles Judah ignored (Leviticus 26:34-35; 2 Chron 36:21). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/25.htm
- Kingcomments adds that Seventy years is the period of a human life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html
- Calvin sees fixing a time limit as a sign of God's fatherly kindness to the faithful remnant: the punishment would only be temporary.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-25.html

**v. 12:**
- When does the seventy years start? Matthew Henry notes some count from Jehoiakim's fourth year and others from Jehoiachin's captivity. He prefers the earlier date.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_025.cfm
- Gill adds up the Babylonian kings' reigns to arrive at the first year of Cyrus.  Poole instead counts from Jehoiachin's captivity.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-12.htm
- Why punish God's own instrument? Calvin says Nebuchadnezzar was called God's servant not because he earned anything, but because God used him without his knowing it.  Benson, quoting Lowth, says the evil was the Babylonians' own and the good that came from it belonged to God alone.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-12.html
- Guzik contrasts Judah's seventy years of desolation with Babylon's permanent one.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/

**v. 13:** Constable notes that some of Jeremiah's prophecies had already been written down by this time. [studylight dcc]

**v. 14:** Feinberg (quoted by Guzik) and Constable say the "many nations and great kings" are the Medes, the Persians and their allies under Cyrus. [enduringword; studylight dcc] Kingcomments says Babylon was judged because Nebuchadnezzar went beyond the Lord's will.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

**vv. 15–16:**
- The cup is a common Old Testament picture of God's wrath (Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17). Thompson suggests it may come from the ordeal-drink test in Numbers 5.
- Guzik connects it to Gethsemane: Jesus drank the cup of fury so that believers would not have to.
- On "stagger", Ryken says the cup is poisonous, not just intoxicating. Kidner applies it to the collective madness that can destroy a nation from within. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-25/]
- Constable says the cup can also stand for blessing, or for a person's lot in life. He reads the action here as a vision, not something Jeremiah literally did. [studylight dcc]
- BibleHub's summary: The cup of wrath points to Christ, who drank judgment so that those who trust Him need not fear the final storm. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/25.htm

**v. 17:** Morgan (quoted by Guzik) describes judgment spreading in widening circles: Judah first, then Babylon, then the nations, then the whole earth. [enduringword] Kingcomments describes Jeremiah obeying an unpleasant task.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

**vv. 18–25:** Constable locates the places on the list:
- Uz lay to the east.
- Dedan and Tema were southeast of Edom; Buz was perhaps in northern Arabia.
- Zimri was perhaps between Arabia and Persia; Elam and Media were east of the Tigris.

He adds that this list is expanded in chapters 46–51. [studylight dcc] The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary links Zimri with Zimran, Abraham's son by Keturah, and says Elam is used in Scripture for Persia generally.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-22.html

**v. 26:**
- "All the kingdoms of the world": Barnes says the "all" here is moral and not geographical (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/jeremiah/25-26.html). Gill says it means the whole Babylonian empire.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-26.htm
- Sheshach: most take it as Babylon written in a code called Atbash, in which the Hebrew alphabet is reversed. Calvin accepts this and points to Jeremiah 51:41, where Sheshach and Babylon stand side by side.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-26.html
- Another view (from Gataker, given in a note to Calvin) says the name came from a Babylonian idol called Shach.  Poole calls such explanations all uncertain guesses (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-26.htm). Gill suggests the code may have been used to avoid provoking Nebuchadnezzar.  (same URL)

**vv. 27–28:** Constable says the doom comes by military conquest and that refusing the message changes nothing. [studylight dcc] Benson's note says that if judgment begins with backsliders, the wicked should not expect to escape.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-26.htm

**v. 29:** Constable links this verse to Amos 3:2 and 1 Peter 4:17. [studylight dcc] BibleHub: Judgment starts with God's own people ("the city that bears My name," v. 29); privilege never exempts from obedience. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/25.htm

**v. 30:** Constable reads the roar as a lion announcing its attack, and thinks reading it as thunder is less likely. He links the winepress to Revelation 14. [studylight dcc]

**v. 31:** Constable sees a lawsuit picture: God holds everyone guilty. [studylight dcc] Kingcomments says God shows that his judgment is lawful.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

**vv. 32–33:** Constable: evil is spreading worldwide, so a global storm of judgment is rising, and the dead lie unburied like manure. [studylight dcc] Kingcomments identifies the sword with the evil that goes forth from nation to nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

**vv. 34–37:** Constable: the shepherds are the leaders. They die along with the flock, break like fine pottery, and cannot escape. [studylight dcc]

**v. 38:** Constable: the Lord leaves his hiding place like a lion, as a Divine Warrior. This verse closes the warnings of chapters 2–25. [studylight dcc] Bridgeway reads it as a lion attacking a flock.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-26.html

## 2. Where the traditions differ

**vv. 11–12, exact or round seventy years:**
- **Literal and exact:** Keil (Lutheran) holds the number is exact.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-25.html Coffman (Church of Christ) goes further and calls the round-number view what unbelievers can come up with (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-25.html).
- **Round number:** Guzik says many scholars, including conservative ones, take it as round or symbolic. [enduringword]
- **Calvin (Reformed)** stresses the pastoral meaning: a limited, fatherly punishment. (Calvin URL above)

**v. 12, a future Babylon (dispensational):** Babylon did not become a complete ruin in 539 BC. Constable reports that literal interpreters therefore expect a future fulfilment (Revelation 17–18), and that some think the city itself must be rebuilt. [studylight dcc] J. Vernon McGee instead says the prophecy has been fulfilled.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-12.html

**vv. 29–38, future Tribulation:** Constable says the final fulfilment awaits Christ's return and the Tribulation judgments (Revelation 6–19). [studylight dcc]

**v. 17, who carries out the disasters:** Kingcomments, an unusual view, says the disasters are carried out by Satan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-25.html

## 3. Modern scholarship (from older critical notes on BibleHub and StudyLight)

- **vv. 12–14:** One commentary on BibleHub says verses 12, 14 and part of 13 cannot be a genuine part of Jeremiah's prophecies, and that verse 12 was built from 29:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-12.htm
- **Septuagint differences:** The Greek text leaves out phrases in verses 9, 12, 13 and 26, including the Sheshach line.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-22.html
- **Sheshach clause (v. 26):** Hastings' Dictionary calls it a conceit of later editors (https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/s/sheshach.html). The Pulpit Commentary also calls the clause a copyist's insertion, while noting the code-name happens to suggest "humiliation".  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/25-26.htm
- **Against this:** Keil argues that verse 12 and 51:41 show the Babylon reference belongs in the text.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/25-22.html
